Computers work with human language constantly and mostly out of sight: a search
box, a spam filter, a translation, a reply that arrives too fast to have been
typed. The field that studies how they do it is called natural language
processing, usually shortened to **NLP**. It covers dozens of connected tasks,
from reading a file without corrupting it to generating a paragraph. Each tile
below is one of them.

## The tasks {#periodic-table-heading}

Related tasks share a column, and the columns run roughly from getting text in,
on the left, through cutting it into usable pieces, to models, generation,
systems, and visual explanation. The arrangement is editorial: position tells
you what a task is filed near and nothing else about it. Laying the field out
at once means a lesson can be found by where it sits rather than by remembering
its name. Thirteen of the eighty-one lessons are written. The rest are planned,
and their tiles stay visible so you can see what is coming.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Start here

Read in number order. Each lesson explains its own idea from the beginning, and
its code assumes the R you have already seen.
:::

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

options(warn = 2)

library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(purrr)
library(stringr)

task_map <- read_csv(
  "data/periodic_table.csv",
  col_types = cols(
    task_number = col_integer(),
    symbol = col_character(),
    title = col_character(),
    item_type = col_character(),
    group_id = col_integer(),
    group_name = col_character(),
    stage = col_character(),
    lesson_path = col_character(),
    status = col_character(),
    last_reviewed = col_character()
  ),
  na = character()
)

available <- task_map |>
  filter(status == "available")

planned <- task_map |>
  filter(status == "planned")

group_sizes <- task_map |>
  count(group_id) |>
  pull(n)

expected_group_sizes <- c(
  7L, 6L, 5L, 5L, 5L,
  6L, 4L, 4L, 5L, 5L,
  5L, 5L, 6L, 6L, 7L
)

lesson_sources <- available |>
  pull(lesson_path) |>
  str_replace("[.]html$", ".qmd")

stopifnot(
  identical(getOption("warn"), 2L),
  inherits(task_map, "tbl_df"),
  identical(task_map$task_number, 1:81),
  identical(sort(unique(task_map$group_id)), 1:15),
  identical(group_sizes, expected_group_sizes),
  identical(which(task_map$status == "available"), 1:13),
  identical(length(unique(task_map$symbol)), 81L),
  all(task_map$status %in% c("available", "planned")),
  all(nzchar(available$lesson_path)),
  all(planned$lesson_path == ""),
  all(nzchar(available$last_reviewed)),
  all(file.exists(lesson_sources))
)

escape_text <- function(value) {
  as.character(htmltools::htmlEscape(value))
}

escape_attribute <- function(value) {
  as.character(
    htmltools::htmlEscape(value, attribute = TRUE)
  )
}

stage_labels <- c(
  source = "Source and training data",
  language = "Language structure",
  model = "Models and analysis",
  generation = "Language generation",
  systems = "Language systems",
  visualization = "Visualization"
)

stopifnot(
  all(unique(task_map$stage) %in% names(stage_labels))
)

render_tile <- function(task_number,
                        symbol,
                        title,
                        item_type,
                        lesson_path,
                        status,
                        ...) {
  is_available <- identical(status, "available")
  label_text <- if (is_available) "Read lesson" else "Planned"
  status_class <- if (is_available) {
    "element-status"
  } else {
    "element-status visually-hidden"
  }

  tile_contents <- sprintf(
    paste0(
      '<span class="element-number">%d</span>',
      '<span class="element-kind">%s</span>',
      '<span class="element-symbol" aria-hidden="true">%s</span>',
      '<span class="element-name">%s</span>',
      '<span class="%s">%s</span>'
    ),
    task_number,
    escape_text(item_type),
    escape_text(symbol),
    escape_text(title),
    status_class,
    label_text
  )

  tile <- if (is_available) {
    sprintf(
      paste0(
        '<a class="nlp-element is-available" ',
        'data-task-number="%d" data-item-type="%s" ',
        'data-status="available" ',
        'href="%s" aria-label="%s">%s</a>'
      ),
      task_number,
      escape_attribute(item_type),
      escape_attribute(lesson_path),
      escape_attribute(
        sprintf(
          "Task %d. %s. Item type: %s. %s.",
          task_number,
          title,
          item_type,
          label_text
        )
      ),
      tile_contents
    )
  } else {
    sprintf(
      paste0(
        '<div class="nlp-element is-planned" ',
        'data-task-number="%d" data-item-type="%s" ',
        'data-status="planned">%s</div>'
      ),
      task_number,
      escape_attribute(item_type),
      tile_contents
    )
  }

  paste0('<li class="element-slot">', tile, "</li>")
}

render_group <- function(group_rows) {
  group_id <- unique(group_rows$group_id)
  group_name <- unique(group_rows$group_name)
  stage <- unique(group_rows$stage)
  stage_label <- unname(stage_labels[stage])
  heading_id <- sprintf("task-group-%d", group_id)

  stopifnot(
    identical(length(group_id), 1L),
    identical(length(group_name), 1L),
    identical(length(stage), 1L),
    identical(length(stage_label), 1L)
  )

  tiles <- group_rows |>
    pmap_chr(render_tile) |>
    paste(collapse = "")

  paste0(
    sprintf(
      '<section class="element-group stage-%s" aria-labelledby="%s">',
      escape_attribute(stage),
      heading_id
    ),
    sprintf(
      paste0(
        '<h3 class="element-group-title" id="%s">',
        '<span class="element-stage">%s</span>',
        '<span class="element-group-name">%s</span>',
        '</h3>'
      ),
      heading_id,
      escape_text(stage_label),
      escape_text(group_name)
    ),
    '<ol class="element-stack">',
    tiles,
    "</ol></section>"
  )
}

stage_key <- stage_labels |>
  imap_chr(function(label, stage) {
    sprintf(
      paste0(
        '<span class="task-map-stage-key-item stage-%s">',
        '<span class="task-map-stage-swatch" aria-hidden="true"></span>',
        '%s</span>'
      ),
      escape_attribute(stage),
      escape_text(label)
    )
  }) |>
  paste(collapse = "")

groups <- task_map |>
  arrange(group_id, task_number) |>
  group_by(group_id) |>
  group_split()

table_html <- groups |>
  map_chr(render_group) |>
  paste(collapse = "")

stopifnot(
  identical(length(groups), 15L),
  identical(
    str_count(table_html, fixed('class="element-slot"')),
    81L
  ),
  identical(
    str_count(table_html, fixed('class="nlp-element is-available"')),
    13L
  )
)

cat(
  '<div class="task-map-key">',
  '<span class="task-map-key-item">',
  '<span class="task-map-key-swatch available" aria-hidden="true"></span>',
  'Read lesson',
  '</span>',
  '<span class="task-map-key-item">',
  '<span class="task-map-key-swatch" aria-hidden="true"></span>',
  'Lesson planned',
  '</span>',
  '</div>',
  '<div class="task-map-stage-key" aria-label="Task stages">',
  stage_key,
  '</div>',
  '<p class="task-map-instructions" id="task-map-instructions">',
  'Select a solid-bordered tile to open its lesson. ',
  'Dashed tiles are planned. If the map is wider than the window, ',
  'use the buttons, arrow keys, or horizontal scrolling.',
  '</p>',
  '<div class="task-map-scroll-controls" ',
  'aria-label="Move through task groups">',
  '<button type="button" data-map-direction="-1" ',
  'aria-controls="nlp-task-map">Earlier groups</button>',
  '<button type="button" data-map-direction="1" ',
  'aria-controls="nlp-task-map">Later groups</button>',
  '</div>',
  '<div class="periodic-scroll" id="nlp-task-map" ',
  'tabindex="0" role="region" ',
  'aria-label="Periodic table of NLP tasks" ',
  'aria-describedby="task-map-instructions">',
  '<div class="periodic-table">',
  table_html,
  '</div></div>',
  sep = ""
)
```

::: {.callout-note}
## What this map is

This is a teaching aid, not a scientific taxonomy or a complete account of the
field. It mixes tasks, methods, objectives, resources, services, applications,
and work done across a model's life. Each tile names its item type so those
differences stay visible. Some inherited group names are broad or imperfect,
and where that happens the lesson says so.
:::

## Why these lessons exist

Your director asks how many of last quarter's 40,000 customer comments are
complaints, because next quarter's support budget depends on the answer. You
hand the comments to an AI assistant. It answers in seconds: 22 percent.

The number might be right. The question is how anyone would know.

Start with the word. Before anything can be counted, someone has to say what a
complaint is. Is a blunt question a complaint? A compliment with one sharp
clause? A report of a broken link? Some answer gets applied to all 40,000
comments, quietly and consistently, whether or not a person chose it. A more
capable model does not settle this, because the difficulty is not what the
model can do. It is what you meant.

Then the margin around it. "About 22 percent" needs the "about" to come from
somewhere. To find out how often an automatic answer is wrong, you compare it
against something you trust more, usually a sample of the same material worked
out by hand and drawn at random so that what you find in it carries over to the
rest. Assumptions can stand in for part of that comparison. Several established
methods estimate error from how far several automatic labellers agree with each
other, and they work. What they buy the estimate with is an assumption about
the shape of the errors, which is itself hard to check without doing some of
the work by hand. A better model shrinks how much you have to check, without
taking the number of checks to zero.

Underneath both is the text itself. Every number about a body of writing is
really a number about the version of that writing which arrived. Characters get
mangled between systems. Rows split at a stray comma. A scanned page reads a
digit as a letter. Sometimes that raises an error. Often it does not, and the
answer changes while continuing to look reasonable. Lessons 1, 3 and 7 each
produce one of these failures on purpose, so you can see what one looks like
from the inside.

Whatever a tool absorbs, something is left over. Here what is left over is
deciding what to measure, on which material, and when to disbelieve the result.
That part has not moved, because it is where the tool gets its instructions and
where its output is accepted or rejected.

You can still buy the work. Labelled data is for sale, annotation vendors are
easy to hire, and a model will label almost anything you give it, while quietly
refusing a few things. Each of those arrives with a number describing how much
its labels agree. Reading that number and knowing what it conceals are
different skills, and in my experience the second comes from having produced
such a number yourself, on your own untidy text, and having watched it flatter
you.

None of this says you must do the work by hand. For drafting, summarising, or
getting a rough sense of an unfamiliar pile of text, these tools already save
real time, and individual failures described in these lessons may well be fixed
in the systems that come next. That case will keep getting stronger. What the
parts named here describe is not a capability gap but the shape of a
measurement: the definition, the comparison, and the text that actually
arrived. How much each one costs is a separate question that depends on your
text and on how much the answer matters, and this page cannot tell you either.

These lessons cover the near end of that work: getting text out of files, web
pages and scans without damaging it, and building a set of hand-checked labels
you can defend. Several also cover the shortcuts, including buying labels,
generating examples, and writing rules, and where each one stops being
trustworthy.

## About this site

**Available** means a lesson exists and its automated checks passed. No lesson
has had final human sign-off yet, and the review record for each one is kept in
`data/lesson_reviews.csv`. Practice in this field moves quickly, so where a
lesson describes current methods rather than settled ground, it says so and
gives a date. The rules a lesson has to meet before it appears here are written
down in
[CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/farach/periodic_table_nlp/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md)
and
[RESEARCH_STANDARDS.md](https://github.com/farach/periodic_table_nlp/blob/main/RESEARCH_STANDARDS.md).

The task names and groupings are adapted from Rob van Zoest's
[Periodic Table of NLP Tasks](https://www.innerdoc.com/periodic-table-of-nlp-tasks/).
That page states no licence and invites reuse. The task names themselves are
standard terms in the field; the grouping, wording, interface, and lessons here
are separate work, and any error in them belongs to this project. If the
original author prefers different terms, this site will follow them.
